title: Nimbus Health Conversational Ops Sandbox Demo

Discussed latency vs cost tradeoffs for real-time triage flows; covered security questions (SOC2, KMS, VPC notes). Agreed next steps: share pricing + sandbox links, run a short throughput test and security packet.

transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: Thu Feb 19 2026 15:00 PST
Duration: 41 minutes
Attendees: Lina T (Redwood AE), Samir P (Redwood SE), Aisha K (Nimbus Head of Platform), Ben M (Nimbus ML Eng), Priya I (Product)

[00:00] Lina (Redwood AE): Hey everybody, thanks for joining. Quick agenda: we'll do a 25 minute walkthrough of hosted Gen/chat, show the console metrics, then a 10 minute Q&A and next steps. Is that good?
[00:18] Aisha (Nimbus): Yep that works. We're really curious about latency and cost for our triage chat where agents push events and we need near-real-time responses.
[00:35] Samir (Redwood SE): Great, I'll start with a quick live demo of streaming so you can see how tokens appear and how we surface partial responses. I'm going to use the sandbox key so nothing hits prod.
[00:52] Samir: (typing) Okay starting a 3-turn convo: prompt + context. You'll see the stream come in in chunks, we flush after every ~32 tokens in this config.
[01:10] Ben (Nimbus): Quick question, do you support both SSE and websockets for streaming? We have a socket-based frontend.
[01:22] Samir: Yes — we support chunked HTTP streaming (SSE-like) and websockets for lower-latency websockets typically give you less overhead but SSE is simpler for some infra. Note: our SDKs wrap both.
[01:36] Priya: Are the partial tokens "committed" for billing or is it only final output?
[01:46] Lina: Token billing is per-generation; partial streamed chunks are part of the generation. The Console breaks down token spend per request so you can see partial vs final tokens in the session trace.
[02:05] Samir: (demo) Here on the Console trace you can see per-token timing, KV cache hit rate, and a latency waterfall. This helps isolate whether the cost is coming from long context or from repeated prompts.
[02:30] Aisha: Nice, that waterfall looks useful. For our use case we often re-use conversation context so cache sounds key. Do you have automatic prefix caching?
[02:45] Samir: We do automatic KV/prefix caching for repeated convo prefixes if you enable the cache policy. It reduces compute by reusing previous KV cache entries. There are also TTL controls if you want to evict old state.
[03:05] Ben: What's the best way to tune generation params for lower latency — temperature, top_p, and truncation?
[03:18] Samir: So start with lower max_tokens and server-side stop sequences. Temperature/top_p mostly affect randomness not latency. The big knobs for latency are: 1) model size/variant, 2) max_tokens, 3) quantized variants or faster kernels. Our Optimize tab will recommend smaller quantized variants if your quality metrics hold.
[03:45] Priya: Can you show the Optimize suggestions?
[03:50] Samir: (navigates) Sure, Optimize runs evaluation on sample prompt sets you upload. It suggests batching, quantization, and routing to cheaper models for non-critical paths. For example it recommended a 4-bit quantized variant for one of our customers with <2% quality regression and 3x cost savings.
[04:20] Aisha: Hmm 3x is interesting — do you support automatic fallback if the quantized variant fails a smoke check?
[04:31] Samir: Yep, we have smart routing and can fallback to a higher-fidelity variant or region if latency/SLO fails. You can set canary windows and automatic rollback based on eval metrics you define.
[04:48] Ben: About retries: what's your recommended retry/backoff pattern? We saw duplicated messages when client-side retried before the server had idempotency keys.
[04:58] Lina: Right, our recommended pattern is client-generated idempotency keys per request_id and then exponential backoff with jitter. For streaming we encourage a resume token pattern — Redwood returns a resume cursor so you can re-request only the missing suffix, but that needs support in your client.
[05:20] Samir: To add, for non-streamed sync calls, use idempotency key + deterministic retry policy. For streaming, we emit granular chunk offsets so the client can request a resume from offset N. Note sometimes the resume offset can be off by a small amount depending on model tokenization — we surface heuristics in the SDK.
[05:45] Priya: Are there built-in client libraries that handle resume and backoff?
[05:52] Samir: Our JS and Python SDKs include helpers for automatic resume and backoff. They also handle request signing and reauth.
[06:05] Aisha: Security touchpoints: do you support SSO/SAML and KMS? We need to bring this into our audit model.
[06:15] Lina: Yes, enterprise Private/Dedicated has SAML/SSO, RBAC, and KMS integrations. For hosted we support customer-managed keys (bring-your-own-KMS) for data at rest encryption in some plans; we'll share the exact matrix in the security packet. We're SOC2 Type II compliant.
[06:35] Ben: What about data residency — our PHI needs to stay in certain regions.
[06:41] Lina: For PHI we'd recommend Redwood Private with a VPC deployment or Dedicated in a region that meets your controls. We'll put together region options in the doc.
[06:55] Samir: Back to the demo — I'm going to intentionally force a transient error to show retries. (simulate 503) You can see the SDK logs an error, then uses the idempotency key and retries after exponential backoff. The Console shows the retry chain and the per-request trace.
[07:20] Ben: The logs show a request_id — can we pipe that into our APM?
[07:26] Samir: Yes, the request_id is returned and also available in the trace. We support linking traces to your APM via headers.
[07:35] Aisha: On billing — does streaming increase cost if you stream partial tokens and then stop? Like if the user abandons mid-stream?
[07:45] Lina: It's billed for tokens generated. If the model generates N tokens before you close the stream, it's billed. One pattern is to prefer shorter max_tokens and have the client-side cancel early and the server not generate extra tokens — but canceling won't retroactively remove tokens already generated.
[08:05] Priya: About throughput — our triage flow needs 150 qps at 300ms p95. Can Redwood hit that in hosted?
[08:16] Samir: Hosted can scale horizontally but p95 300ms for complex models is challenging on large contexts. You have options: 1) dedicated pool sized for that SLO, 2) quantized/faster model variants, 3) prefix caching and batch warmers. For a 300ms p95 you'd likely want a dedicated plan or aggressive quantization plus warm workers. We'll run a benchmark with your prompts.
[08:45] Ben: Okay let's schedule that.
[08:49] Samir: I'll collect sample prompt traces from you and run a 30m throughput test under 5 concurrent clients to mimic your triage pattern.
[09:00] Lina: I'm going to demo the Console Alerting briefly: you can set token burn alerts, latency SLO alerts, and quality regressions tied to eval sets. If Optimize flags a drop in rouge/emscore we can auto-block a rollout.
[09:20] Aisha: That auto-block sounds helpful. Do you integrate with PagerDuty?
[09:26] Lina: Yup, webhooks to PagerDuty/Slack, and you can hook to the Console's incident actions.
[09:34] Samir: (demo) Now I'll show param tuning live: first run with max_tokens=256, temp=0.7, second run with max_tokens=64 and temp=0.2 to see behavior. Notice the token emission rate and overall latency drop when max_tokens is smaller.
[10:00] Ben: Any advice on truncation and context window management?
[10:08] Samir: Use sliding window + semantic dedupe to keep the most relevant context. If you have a structured state store, only materialize necessary history into the prompt. Console can show which context tokens add the most latency.
[10:30] Priya: For the triage flow we do stepwise retrieval, is there a recommended batching scheme?
[10:38] Samir: For retrieval + generation patterns, batch retrievals server-side and fan-out small generation requests. We recommend batching generation requests when possible, but for low-latency user-facing flows smaller batches reduce tail latency. Optimize will recommend batching thresholds based on your observed latency histogram.
[11:05] Aisha: Can we see an example of a fallback policy? Like when model fails, route to cheaper model or return a canned response?
[11:14] Samir: (shares config) In the Console you set a route policy: if latency > X or error rate > Y, route to fallback model or canned answer. You can also define per-route retry windows and circuit-breakers.
[11:34] Ben: Regarding SDKs, are they open source? Can we fork to instrument?
[11:40] Lina: Our SDKs are MIT-ish in the developer docs but certain enterprise integrations are internal. We'll share the SDK repo links for your engineering review.
[11:53] Priya: A bit nitty — how do you handle tokenization differences across model variants for resume offsets? We saw off-by-one issues in another provider.
[12:05] Samir: Good point — resume offsets are token-based. When routing between variants, tokenization can differ. Our resume heuristics include a small overlap window and optional alignments. In worst-case we re-gen a small suffix to avoid semantic drift. We'll include the gotchas doc in the packet.
[12:30] Aisha: Can we get a read-only Console link to see telemetry after the call?
[12:34] Lina: Yes, we'll enable a sandbox Console tenant read-only for your team and send the link.
[12:40] Ben: On security again — for hosted, where are logs stored and how long? We need 90-day retention and audit logs.
[12:48] Lina: Hosted has configurable retention; by default logs are 30 days, enterprise add-on for longer retention. Audit logs are available for Dedicated/Private with extended retention. We'll include the retention matrix.
[13:05] Samir: (demo) Now I want to show an edge-case: a mid-stream partial generation then a client reconnect. You can see resume cursor X and how the SDK requests offset X+1 and stitches output. There's a small duplicate token sometimes, that's why we expose de-dupe helpers.
[13:36] Priya: That's okay as long as it's dedupe-able.
[13:40] Aisha: Anything else on retries? We have a regulatory constraint on duplicate outputs for notifications, so idempotency is critical.
[13:49] Lina: Then we'll insist on idempotency keys at the message level and server-side checks to avoid duplicate side effects. For notification flows do-read/confirm patterns and persist dedupe keys.
[14:05] Samir: (typing) I'm going to switch to showing an example logging trace: request start, model compile time, kernel selection, first token emitted at 120ms, KV hit rate 87%, total tokens 48.
[14:28] Ben: Kernel selection — is that automatic? Can we pin kernels?
[14:34] Samir: Kernel selection is automatic in the runtime. For Private/Dedicated we can expose kernel selection hints if you need deterministic execution for reproducibility.
[14:50] Aisha: How does billing work for model variants? If Optimize routes to cheaper variant does it change the billing line?
[14:58] Lina: Billing is per model-variant per token. The Console shows unit price per variant and the routing logic keeps a cost ledger so you can see aggregate savings.
[15:14] Samir: I want to show the Console's token-level breakdown for a sample session — it's grouped by prompt tokens vs gen tokens and shows cost per token.
[15:28] Priya: Cool, that will help our finance team forecast.
[15:34] Ben: On latency guarantees — do you provide SLAs for hosted?
[15:40] Lina: Hosted API has best-effort performance. For SLA-backed p95/p99 targets we recommend Dedicated with reserved capacity. We can propose a Dedicated plan if you need contractual SLOs.
[15:55] Aisha: We might start hosted for devs then move to Dedicated for production.
[16:00] Lina: That's a common path. Sandbox->pilot->dedicated.
[16:06] Samir: One more demo: I'm toggling a fallback policy to route only non-PHI requests to cheaper models while PHI requests stay pinned to the verified variant. This is policy-based routing by tag.
[16:27] Priya: Nice, that helps keep cost down without compromising PHI handling.
[16:33] Ben: Any caveats about cold start for large models?
[16:38] Samir: Cold start exists for large models; charge a small cold-start latency. We have warmers and prewarmed pools for Dedicated and private deployments. Also continuous batching can hide some cold-starts.
[16:58] Aisha: Our timeline — we'd like a pilot in 4 weeks. Is that realistic?
[17:04] Lina: Yes, 4-week pilot is doable. Next steps: we'll send pricing, enable sandbox Console, and Samir will run a benchmark once we get sample prompts.
[17:15] Ben: For the bench, we'll provide a small dataset and two typical convo traces.
[17:20] Samir: Great.
[17:22] Speaker 6: (faint) sorry I'm joining late—
[17:28] Priya: No problem.
[17:30] Samir: Switching to Q&A — feel free to ask anything we didn't cover.
[17:36] Ben: Do you have a recommended pattern for batching vs single requests in a mobile client?
[17:41] Samir: On mobile prefer single small requests to keep battery and latency low; do server-side batching at API gateway if you can. Mobile user-facing UX prioritizes p95 latency.
[17:55] Aisha: About Optimize: how does it evaluate quality regressions? We use an internal scoring metric.
[18:02] Samir: You can upload your scoring function or example eval set; Optimize runs cross-variant comparisons and reports delta metrics. It supports custom metrics as well.
[18:20] Priya: One more: do you have a sandbox data deletion guarantee? We need ephemeral test data removed after pilot.
[18:29] Lina: We can set sandbox tenants with auto-delete after X days. For Hosted we can also do per-tenant data wipes on request; we'll document retention APIs.
[18:45] Ben: Any major limitations we should know?
[18:49] Samir: Biggest tradeoffs are model selection vs latency. If you need sub-300ms p95 on large-context generation, you either need heavy engineering or Dedicated/quantization tradeoffs. Also resume offsets across variants have minor edge-cases.
[19:07] Aisha: Fair.
[19:10] Lina: Let's recap next steps — Lina to send pricing + security packet, Samir to run bench after receiving prompts, Aisha to send compliance requests.
[19:22] Ben: Perfect.
[19:25] Priya: Thanks, this was super helpful.
[19:28] Lina: Thanks all — we'll follow up with links and an invite for the benchmark session.
[19:34] (meeting ends)

Notes on transcript quality: occasional overlap, some product names transcribed incorrectly (e.g., "Consoel" instead of Console), and minor filler words preserved.
